## Goal

After this exercise you will be able to:

- Translate a small biology mixture problem into a system of linear equations
  and write it as $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$.
- Solve $2\times 2$ and $3\times 3$ systems **by hand** using substitution and
  Gaussian elimination with an augmented matrix.
- Compute the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix by row-reducing $[\,A \mid I\,]$
  to $[\,I \mid A^{-1}\,]$, and use it to solve for several measurement vectors.
- Check a solution by substituting it back into the original equations.
- Reproduce your by-hand answers in R with [`solve`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/solve.html).

This is the by-hand fluency you need for the written exam, so do the pen-and-
paper parts *before* you touch R.

## Background

A **bulk** sample is a mixture of cell types. If we know, for each cell type,
how much signal it contributes to each measured gene (its *signature*), then
the total measured signal is a weighted sum of the unknown cell-type amounts.
With as many genes measured as cell types present, recovering the amounts is
exactly solving a square linear system.

In standard form,
$$
A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b},
$$
where the column $j$ of $A$ is the signature of cell type $j$, the entry
$x_j$ is the unknown amount of cell type $j$, and $\mathbf{b}$ holds the bulk
measurements. Row $i$ of the system reads
$$
A_{i1}x_1 + A_{i2}x_2 + \dots + A_{in}x_n = b_i,
$$
the total signal for gene $i$.

Two solution methods:

- **Substitution** — solve one equation for one unknown and substitute into
  the others. Good for $2\times 2$.
- **Gaussian elimination** — use row operations (multiply a row by a non-zero
  number; add a multiple of one row to another) to reach **upper-triangular**
  form, then **back-substitute** from the bottom row up. Scales to any size.

## By hand

Do these on paper. Show the row operations, not just the final numbers.

### Problem 1 — a 2×2 mixture (substitution)

A blood sample is a mix of two cell types. Per unit, their signatures for
genes G1 and G2 are:

| | Type A | Type B |
|--|:--:|:--:|
| G1 | 3 | 1 |
| G2 | 1 | 2 |

The bulk measurements are G1 $= 11$ and G2 $= 7$.

(a) Write the system as two equations and as $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$.
(b) Solve for the amounts $x$ (Type A) and $y$ (Type B) by **substitution**.
(c) **Check** your answer in both original equations.

### Problem 2 — the same 2×2 by Gaussian elimination

Re-solve Problem 1 using **Gaussian elimination on the augmented matrix**
$[\,A \mid \mathbf{b}\,]$. Reach upper-triangular form, then back-substitute.
You should of course get the same answer as in Problem 1.

### Problem 3 — a 3×3 mixture (Gaussian elimination)

Three cell types (amounts $x$, $y$, $z$), three marker genes give the system
$$
\begin{aligned}
1x + 2y + 1z &= 8\\
2x + 1y + 1z &= 7\\
1x + 1y + 3z &= 10
\end{aligned}
$$

(a) Write the augmented matrix $[\,A \mid \mathbf{b}\,]$.
(b) Eliminate column 1, then column 2, to reach upper-triangular form.
(c) Back-substitute to find $x$, $y$, $z$, and **check** all three equations.

### Problem 4 — the inverse with an augmented matrix

Use the signature matrix $A$ from Problem 1.

(a) Write the augmented matrix $[\,A \mid I\,]$ and row-reduce it until the left
side is $I$. Read off $A^{-1}$.
(b) Check that $A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{b} = (11, 7)$ gives your answer from Problem 1.
(c) A second blood sample, with the same two cell types, measures G1 $= 8$ and
G2 $= 6$. Find its amounts with **one** matrix–vector multiplication, and check them.

## Explore {#explore}

Write the two equations as $ax + by = c$ and $dx + ey = f$ (here $x$ and $y$ are the amounts from Problem 1). Each equation is a line in the $(x, y)$ plane, and a solution is a point on both lines. The picture below starts with the system from Problem 1 (R1 blue, R2 orange). Use the sliders, or drag the open circle on a line to shift it and the filled circle to turn it. The grey box shows the elimination step $\text{R2} - m\,\text{R1}$ with the current numbers.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="twolines" data-eq1="3 1 11" data-eq2="1 2 7"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/twolines.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Compare the crossing point and the grey box with your answers to Problems 1 and 2.

**E2.** Keep R1 and set $d = 1.5$, $e = 0.5$. Now move only $f$. For which value of $f$ are there infinitely many solutions? What does elimination leave for any other value, for example $f = 4$?

**E3.** Click *reset*. Explain why changing **only** $f$ can never give a system with no solution. How far does the crossing point move when $f$ changes by $0.5$?

**E4.** Click *nearly parallel* ($x + y = 2$, $x + 1.1y = 2.5$). Where do the lines cross? Move $f$ from $2.5$ to $3$. Where is the crossing now, and how does the jump compare with E3? What would this mean for a mixture of two cell types with almost the same signature?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**E1.** The lines cross at $(x, y) = (3, 2)$, the answer to Problem 1. The box shows $\text{R2} - (1/3)\,\text{R1}$, which leaves $0x + 1.667y = 3.333$, that is $\tfrac53 y = \tfrac{10}{3}$ as in Problem 2, so $y = 2$ and $x = 3$.

**E2.** $f = 5.5$. Then R2 $= 1.5x + 0.5y = 5.5$ is exactly $\tfrac12\times$R1, the same line drawn twice. $\text{R2} - \tfrac12\text{R1}$ leaves $0 = 0$, so $y$ is free and every point on the line is a solution. For any other $f$ the lines are parallel and distinct: with $f = 4$ the step leaves $0 = 4 - 5.5 = -1.5$, which is impossible, so there is no solution.

**E3.** $f$ only shifts line R2 sideways; its slope stays the same. Two lines with different slopes always cross exactly once, wherever they are. A change of $0.5$ in $f$ moves the crossing from $(3, 2)$ to $(2.9, 2.3)$, a distance of about $0.32$.

**E4.** They cross at $(-3, 5)$. With $f = 3$ the crossing jumps to $(-8, 10)$, off the plot: a move of about $7.07$ for the same change of $0.5$, more than 20 times as far as in E3. The lines are only $2.7^\circ$ apart, so a small shift of one line slides the crossing a long way along the other. For a mixture, two almost identical signatures mean a little measurement noise in $\mathbf{b}$ gives very different estimated amounts.
:::

## In R

Use R only to **verify** the answers you already found by hand.

```r
# Problem 1 / 2 — the 2x2 system
A <- matrix(c(3, 1,
              1, 2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
b <- c(11, 7)

x <- solve(A, b)   # solve A x = b
x
# expected: your Type A and Type B amounts from the by-hand answer

# Check: does A %*% x reproduce b?
A %*% x
```

```r
# Problem 3 — the 3x3 system
A3 <- matrix(c(1, 2, 1,
               2, 1, 1,
               1, 1, 3), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
b3 <- c(8, 7, 10)

x3 <- solve(A3, b3)
x3

# Verify the residual is (numerically) zero
A3 %*% x3 - b3
```

```r
# Problem 4 — the inverse
Ainv <- solve(A)    # one argument: the inverse
Ainv
Ainv %*% A          # the identity
Ainv %*% c(8, 6)    # the second sample
```

Note `byrow = TRUE`: it fills the matrix row by row, so the R code reads in the
same order as the equations on paper. (The default, `byrow = FALSE`, fills
column by column — a common source of confusion.)

## Hints

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — setting up A and b"}
Each **equation** is one **row**. The numbers multiplying the unknowns ($x$, $y$, ...) go
into $A$ in order; the right-hand number goes into $\mathbf{b}$. For Problem 1,
the two equations are $3x + 1y = 11$ and $1x + 2y = 7$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — substitution"}
From the second equation of Problem 1, $x = 7 - 2y$. Substitute that into
the first equation to get a single equation in $y$ alone, solve it, then
back-substitute to get $x$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — choosing the elimination multiplier"}
To kill the entry in row $i$, column $j$ using a pivot row $p$ (which has a
non-zero entry in column $j$), use
$$
\text{R}_i \;\leftarrow\; \text{R}_i - \frac{A_{ij}}{A_{pj}}\,\text{R}_p .
$$
Apply the operation to the **whole** augmented row, including the $\mathbf{b}$
entry.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 4 — back-substitution"}
After reaching upper-triangular form, the **last** row has only one unknown —
solve it. Carry that value into the row above, which now also has one remaining
unknown, and continue upward.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 5 — the inverse with [A | I]"}
Work in three stages: (1) clear the entry **below** the diagonal, exactly as in
Problem 2; (2) clear the entry **above** the diagonal, using row 2 to change
row 1; (3) divide each row by its diagonal number so the left side becomes $I$.
Every operation acts on all four numbers in the row. Check with
$A^{-1}A = I$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 6 — the R functions"}
[`matrix`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/matrix.html) builds a matrix (use
`byrow = TRUE`); [`solve`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/solve.html) with two arguments
solves $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, and with one argument, `solve(A)`, returns $A^{-1}$;
[`%*%`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/matmult.html) is matrix multiplication, used here
to check the answer.
:::

## Solutions

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}

### Problem 1 — substitution

(a) Equations: $3x + y = 11$ and $x + 2y = 7$. In standard form,
$$
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} 11 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

(b) From equation 2, $x = 7 - 2y$. Substitute into equation 1:
$$
3(7 - 2y) + y = 11 \;\Rightarrow\; 21 - 6y + y = 11
\;\Rightarrow\; -5y = -10 \;\Rightarrow\; y = 2.
$$
Then $x = 7 - 2(2) = 3$. So **$x = 3$ (Type A), $y = 2$ (Type B)**.

(c) Check: $3(3) + 1(2) = 11\ \checkmark$ and $1(3) + 2(2) = 7\ \checkmark$.

### Problem 2 — Gaussian elimination

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 3 & 1 & 11 \\ 1 & 2 & 7 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}-\frac13\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 3 & 1 & 11 \\ 0 & \tfrac{5}{3} & \tfrac{10}{3} \end{array}\right]
$$
Bottom row: $\tfrac{5}{3}y = \tfrac{10}{3} \Rightarrow y = 2$.
Back-substitute into R1: $3x + 2 = 11 \Rightarrow x = 3$. Same answer.

### Problem 3 — 3×3 Gaussian elimination

(a) Augmented matrix:
$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 2 & 1 & 8\\
2 & 1 & 1 & 7\\
1 & 1 & 3 & 10
\end{array}\right]
$$

(b) Clear column 1 with $\text{R2}-2\text{R1}$ and $\text{R3}-\text{R1}$:
$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 2 & 1 & 8\\
0 & -3 & -1 & -9\\
0 & -1 & 2 & 2
\end{array}\right]
$$
Clear column 2 with $\text{R3} - \tfrac{1}{3}\text{R2}$
(since $-1 = \tfrac{1}{3}\cdot(-3)$):
$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 2 & 1 & 8\\
0 & -3 & -1 & -9\\
0 & 0 & \tfrac{7}{3} & 5
\end{array}\right]
$$
(Row 3: $2 - \tfrac13(-1) = \tfrac{7}{3}$ and $2 - \tfrac13(-9) = 5$.)

(c) Back-substitute:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\tfrac{7}{3}z &= 5 &&\Rightarrow\; z = \tfrac{15}{7}\approx 2.143\\
-3y - z &= -9 &&\Rightarrow\; -3y = -9 + \tfrac{15}{7} = -\tfrac{48}{7}
   \;\Rightarrow\; y = \tfrac{16}{7}\approx 2.286\\
x + 2y + z &= 8 &&\Rightarrow\; x = 8 - \tfrac{32}{7} - \tfrac{15}{7}
   = 8 - \tfrac{47}{7} = \tfrac{9}{7}\approx 1.286
\end{aligned}
$$
So $x = \tfrac{9}{7},\ y = \tfrac{16}{7},\ z = \tfrac{15}{7}$.

Check equation 1: $\tfrac{9}{7} + 2\cdot\tfrac{16}{7} + \tfrac{15}{7}
= \tfrac{9 + 32 + 15}{7} = \tfrac{56}{7} = 8\ \checkmark$.
(Equations 2 and 3 check out the same way.)

### Problem 4 — the inverse

(a) Clear below the diagonal (as in Problem 2), make the second pivot 1, clear
above it, then scale row 1:
$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 3 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}-\frac13\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 3 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac53 & -\tfrac13 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,\times\,\frac35\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 3 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -\tfrac15 & \tfrac35 \end{array}\right]
$$
$$
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}-\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 3 & 0 & \tfrac65 & -\tfrac35 \\ 0 & 1 & -\tfrac15 & \tfrac35 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,\div\,3\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & \tfrac25 & -\tfrac15 \\ 0 & 1 & -\tfrac15 & \tfrac35 \end{array}\right]
$$
So $A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.4 & -0.2 \\ -0.2 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$.
Check: $A^{-1}A = \begin{pmatrix} 0.4\cdot3 - 0.2\cdot1 & 0.4\cdot1 - 0.2\cdot2 \\ -0.2\cdot3 + 0.6\cdot1 & -0.2\cdot1 + 0.6\cdot2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. $\checkmark$

(b) $A^{-1}\mathbf{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.4\cdot 11 - 0.2\cdot 7 \\ -0.2\cdot 11 + 0.6\cdot 7 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$, as in Problem 1.

(c) $A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3.2 - 1.2 \\ -1.6 + 3.6 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$: 2 units of Type A and 2 of Type B.
Check: G1 $= 3\cdot2 + 1\cdot2 = 8$ and G2 $= 1\cdot2 + 2\cdot2 = 6$. $\checkmark$
The inverse was computed once and reused; with many samples that saves redoing the elimination each time.

### R verification

```r
A <- matrix(c(3, 1, 1, 2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
b <- c(11, 7)
solve(A, b)
# [1] 3 2

A3 <- matrix(c(1, 2, 1,
               2, 1, 1,
               1, 1, 3), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
b3 <- c(8, 7, 10)
solve(A3, b3)
# [1] 1.285714 2.285714 2.142857   (= 9/7, 16/7, 15/7)

A3 %*% solve(A3, b3) - b3
# all entries ~0 (tiny floating-point residual)

solve(A)
#      [,1] [,2]
# [1,]  0.4 -0.2
# [2,] -0.2  0.6
solve(A) %*% c(8, 6)
# [1,] 2
# [2,] 2
```

:::

## Where this leads

Every system in the by-hand problems had **exactly one** solution. As the Explore section shows, that is not guaranteed:
**Linear systems in R** builds these systems and asks what happens when $A$ is
*singular* or *non-square* — the cases of **no solution** and **infinitely
many solutions**, which correspond to a deconvolution problem being
over- or under-determined.
